---
title: "Disclosure determined by tier sizes"
subtitle: "3.2 · after the postrank theory book, ch. 9, 16 and 17"
description: "How many pairwise directions are stated for each pattern of tier sizes."
---

A report with three balanced tiers states more pairwise directions than a report with two small tiers and one large
tier. In both reports, units in different tiers are ranked and units in the same tier are left unranked. The
number of pairs in each category follows from the tier sizes. The distribution counts how many ordered size
patterns yield each disclosure count. It holds the number of units and tiers fixed and gives each valid size
pattern equal weight.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Balanced thirty.** Sizes 10, 10, 10 state 300 of 435 pairs, a share of .690. Each withheld triangle contributes
  its within-tier count to the grouped formula. Balanced sizes reach the maximum for this number of tiers.
- **Two tiny tiers.** Sizes 1, 1, 28 state only 57 pairs, although they use the same number of tiers. The balanced
  reference still states 300. Moving the smallest tiers to another position gives the same disclosure but another
  ordered size pattern.
- **Four tiers.** Sizes 8, 7, 8, 7 state 337 pairs (.775). These tiers reach the largest possible disclosure when four tiers share thirty units.
- **Balanced twelve.** Three groups of four state 48 of 66 pairs. Enter another size vector or move the individual controls to compare groups with the same total.
- **Unbalanced twelve.** Sizes 5, 4, 3 state 47 pairs, below the balanced maximum of 48. A zero size or incorrect total is invalid; the result remains unavailable until the vector is feasible.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The distribution includes every ordered size pattern with at least one unit per tier. A pattern is counted once
regardless of how many ways the units could be assigned to it. Quantile rules usually produce nearly balanced
sizes, although postrank can merge neighboring tiers to keep equal estimates together. The formula gives the
exact number of comparisons for any valid sizes. To assess their accuracy, we would also need the assignments
and the probabilities for the pairs they disclose.
:::
